A one-session seminar · Hebrew Bible and the Persian age

Chronicles: History Rewritten, and the Work of Sara Japhet

What the biblical books of Chronicles are, how their author worked, what Sara Japhet and other scholars have argued, and how much of the book can be called history

Prepared by Scholar · 16 November 2026

One session · about two and a quarter hours · seven parts

This seminar covers the biblical books of Chronicles (in Hebrew, Divrei ha-Yamim) in a single sitting. It reads the work as a piece of history-writing from the Persian or early Hellenistic age (roughly the fifth to the third century BCE). It gives the scholarship of Sara Japhet (1934–2024) the central place and sets it beside the other major voices in the field. The approach is historical and literary. It is not devotional.

Every page of the seminar follows the same rules. Each specific fact (a date, a title, a year of publication, a verse number) was checked against at least one source that does not depend on Wikipedia, or it is marked [unconfirmed] in the text. Quotations were copied from texts I actually opened, and the page number is given where the text has one. Where scholars disagree, the page names the scholars and does not choose for you.

How claims are tagged

  • confirmed Checked in a primary record, or in two sources that do not depend on each other. Wikipedia did not count.
  • disputed Scholars disagree. The page names them.
  • unsupported No source I opened supports the claim. It appears only so that it can be set aside.
  • estimate A number or date that is rounded, calculated or approximate.
  • [unconfirmed] I could not check the point against an independent source.

Hebrew verse texts come from Sefaria (the Hebrew is “Miqra according to the Masorah”; the English is the Jewish Publication Society translation of 1917, which is in the public domain). Japhet’s commentary is cited by the printed page numbers of the 1993 edition. In the side-by-side tables, this color marks words that differ between the two books and this color marks a clause that both books keep.

The short answer

What it is. Chronicles retells the history of Israel from Adam to the edict of Cyrus. It leans heavily on Samuel and Kings and changes them on purpose [Japhet 1993, p. 8]. confirmed

What Japhet argued. One author wrote Chronicles, and that author did not write Ezra–Nehemiah. The book is a general account of how divine justice governs history, and it was written “at the end of the fourth century BCE” [Japhet 1993, pp. 4, 7, 28]. disputed

What is still open. The date (the proposals span over four hundred years), the number of authors, the Hebrew text the author copied from, and how much of the book reports real events [Japhet 1993, p. 24]. disputed

The nineteenth-century setting. De Wette’s essay of 1806 made Chronicles the test of whether the law of Moses was early, and Wellhausen began his history of Israel from it. Zunz (1832) first argued that one writer made Chronicles and Ezra [de Wette 1806, p. 135] [Wellhausen 1883, p. 177] [Zunz 1832, p. 21]. confirmed

Why it matters. It is the only full “second telling” of Israel’s monarchy inside the Hebrew Bible. Comparing it with Samuel and Kings shows how a community in the Persian province of Judah rewrote its own past.

Four corrections to common statements

  • Wellhausen’s title. His book of 1878 was called Geschichte Israels, Band I. The title Prolegomena zur Geschichte Israels belongs to the second edition of 1883, and the English translation of 1885 uses it [Encyclopedia.com]. confirmed
  • The “one author” idea is older than Noth. Leopold Zunz proposed in 1832 that the Chronicler also wrote Ezra–Nehemiah, and F. C. Movers reached the same view in 1834 [Japhet 1993, p. 3]. Martin Noth’s work came in 1943 and built on a view already standard. confirmed
  • Gramberg sided with de Wette. A recent survey lists Gramberg’s book of 1823 among the attacks on de Wette. His preface says he aims to justify the result of Gesenius and de Wette and to defend it against Dahler [Gramberg 1823, p. VII] (Part 3). confirmed
  • Publication details differ between sources. Japhet’s 1968 article runs pp. 330–371 in the JSTOR header and pp. 332–72 in her own bibliography. Her Hebrew book is dated 1977 by the Hebrew University and 1978 by Eisenbrauns. See the full list at the end.

1Part one

What Chronicles is

Name · canon · contents · time range · about 10 minutes

1.1 The name

The Hebrew title is דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים, Divrei ha-Yamim, “the events (or the words) of the days.” The title names a kind of book, a chronicle. The Hebrew Bible uses the same phrase for royal records that no longer exist: “the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel” (1 Kings 14:19), “of the Kings of Judah” (1 Kings 14:29), “of the Kings of Media and Persia” (Esther 10:2), and “the chronicles of King David” (1 Chr 27:24) [Japhet 1993, p. 1] [I Kings.14.19 on Sefaria] [I Kings.14.29 on Sefaria] [Esther.10.2 on Sefaria] [I Chronicles.27.24 on Sefaria]. confirmed

The book does not name itself. Japhet reports that the earliest attested names are in rabbinic sources (the Mishnah, the Talmud and the Midrash), and that the rabbis also called it “the Book of Genealogies” (Pesaḥim 62b) [Japhet 1993, p. 1]. confirmed for the verse checks above; the rabbinic citations rest on Japhet alone [unconfirmed].

The Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible) titles the book Paraleipomena, “things left over” or “omitted.” Japhet observes that this title describes what the translators thought the book contained, not its genre, and that it “may carry negative connotations” [Japhet 1993, p. 1]. Jerome preferred chronikon, and “it is probably through Jerome’s suggestion and influence that ‘Chronicles’ was taken up by most modern translations” [Japhet 1993, p. 1]. confirmed on Japhet’s authority; I did not open Jerome’s prologue [unconfirmed].

1.2 Its place in the canon

The canon is the list of books a community treats as authoritative. The Hebrew Bible has three divisions: Torah, Prophets and Writings (Ketuvim). Chronicles sits in the Writings, but its position there varies:

  • A Talmudic baraitha (a teaching from the early rabbinic period) lists Chronicles last among the Writings (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 14b). Most manuscripts and printed editions follow that order [Japhet 1993, p. 2].
  • Two of the oldest and best Masoretic manuscripts, the Leningrad Codex and the Aleppo Codex, place it first among the Writings, and the Masoretic notes follow the same order [Japhet 1993, p. 2]. The Aleppo scan on Wikimedia Commons is labeled “Ketuvim 1 – Chronicles” [Commons file description]. confirmed
  • The standard scholarly editions of the Hebrew Bible (Biblia Hebraica Kittel and Stuttgartensia), which print the Leningrad text, move Chronicles to the end, “succumbing to the more dominant Babylonian tradition” [Japhet 1993, p. 2]. confirmed

Japhet adds that “either of the two locations … may be well justified”: as a comprehensive history of the people, Chronicles can open the Writings or close them [Japhet 1993, p. 2].

1.3 Contents

Japhet divides the book into three parts that differ in content, in literary form and in emphasis [Japhet 1993, p. 8]:

  1. 1 Chr 1–9, an introduction made of genealogies and lists. It runs from Adam to the twelve sons of Jacob, then through the tribes, and ends with the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
  2. 1 Chr 10 – 2 Chr 9, the history of Israel under David and then Solomon. David’s part has four sub-units, Solomon’s three [Japhet 1993, p. 10].
  3. 2 Chr 10–36, the history of the kingdom of Judah from the break with the northern tribes.

Figure 3 shows how the 1,765 verses divide. Sefaria’s Masoretic verse numbering gives 943 verses in 1 Chronicles and 822 in 2 Chronicles [1 Chr on Sefaria] [2 Chr on Sefaria]. confirmed estimate for the verse counts per part, which I added up from the chapter lengths in that numbering. The second bar uses the figure of 558 verses with a “recognized, known parallel” in Samuel or Kings [Endres et al., via arXiv, section 4.1]. disputed: counts of “parallel” verses vary with the rules used, and I saw only the citing paper, not the 1998 synopsis [unconfirmed].

1.4 The time range

Chronicles describes Israel’s history “from beginning to ‘beginning’ — from the inception of human existence with Adam, through the destruction of the first commonwealth during the reign of Zedekiah, to the new commencement with the declaration of Cyrus” [Japhet 1993, p. 8]. The book ends with that declaration (2 Chr 36:22–23). The edict is dated to the first year of Cyrus, and Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BCE according to the British Museum’s catalog entry for the Cyrus Cylinder [British Museum] [2 Chr 36:22–23 on Sefaria]. confirmed

The narrated time (Adam to Cyrus) is a different thing from the time of writing. The book was composed long after the last events it tells. Part 5 sets out the proposed dates.

Key dates
  1. 539 BCECyrus takes Babylon; the edict in 2 Chr 36:22–23 is dated to his first year.
  2. 6th–2nd c. BCERange of proposed dates of writing, over four hundred years (Welch to the Maccabean period); the most common view is the fourth century (Japhet, p. 24; Part 5).
  3. 1832Zunz: the Chronicler also wrote Ezra–Nehemiah.
  4. 1968Japhet reopens the question of common authorship.
  5. 1993Japhet’s commentary, still the standard English work.
Why it matters

Chronicles is the last major biblical history in time of writing, yet it covers the earliest events. Because it sits at the end of a long chain of earlier books, it shows how those books were read by the first people to treat them as a library.

2Part two

Sources and method

Four passages side by side · named sources · the text behind Samuel · about 20 minutes

2.1 The Chronicler’s library

The author of Chronicles is anonymous, and scholars call him “the Chronicler.” Japhet describes his working method this way: “Because of his peculiar literary method of employing and citing earlier works, the ‘library’ which was available to the Chronicler may be easily reconstructed” [Japhet 1993, p. 27]. That library includes the whole Pentateuch, the books of Samuel and Kings (which scholars call the Deuteronomistic history, a long history of Israel shaped by the outlook of the book of Deuteronomy), and also Zechariah, Lamentations, and two passages taken from Ezra–Nehemiah: the edict of Cyrus (Ezra 1:1–3a) and a list of the inhabitants of Jerusalem (Neh 11:3–19) [Japhet 1993, p. 27]. confirmed on Japhet’s authority; I checked the Cyrus passages in the text myself (Table 1, below).

Most of what Chronicles shares with another book it shares with Samuel and Kings. Japhet calls this the “synoptic” nature of the book: much of it “represents a literal citation of earlier biblical” text [Japhet 1993, p. 28]. Her own description of the technique, from her note on 2 Chronicles 32, is worth keeping in mind for every table below: the Chronicler uses “the Deuteronomistic story of Kings as his point of departure on the one hand, and the extensive reworking through omissions, additions, rephrasing and epitomization on the other” [Japhet 1993, p. 976]. confirmed

And he prayed unto Him; and He was entreated of him, and heard his supplication, and brought him back to Jerusalem into his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew that the LORD He was God.

What the differences mean has been argued for 150 years. Here are the main readings.

A. The census (2 Sam 24:1 and 1 Chr 21:1)

  • Wellhausen (1878; English 1885) lists the change as one of many “improving touches”: instead of “the anger of Jehovah was kindled against Israel, and he moved David,” Chronicles has “Satan stood up against Israel and moved David” [Wellhausen 1885, p. 179]. He also notes that David pays “600 shekels of gold” where Samuel has “50 shekels of silver”: “to make the king pay right royally costs the Chronicler nothing” [Wellhausen 1885, p. 179]. confirmed for what he wrote.
  • Japhet reads the change differently. She grants that the Chronicler removed God’s anger and gave the incitement to “another agent,” so that “David himself is presented as exclusively responsible” [Japhet 1993, p. 373]. But she doubts that satan here is a proper name. The word has no article, and in the Hebrew Bible a common noun becomes a proper name by taking the article; so she reads it as “an adversary” and calls the anonymous figure “the antithesis of Joab,” who tries to dissuade David [Japhet 1993, pp. 374–376]. She also notes that nowhere else in Chronicles does an independent power of evil appear [Japhet 1993, p. 375]. disputed: most English translations print “Satan” [Japhet 1993, p. 374], and Japhet argues against that reading.

B. Bathsheba (2 Sam 11 – 12 and 1 Chr 20:1)

Chronicles keeps the sentence “But David tarried at Jerusalem,” but the story that sentence introduces in Samuel is gone. Wellhausen’s explanation: the Chronicler omits what “does not contribute much to the glorification of the king,” and the result in 1 Chr 20:1 is “meaningless” [Wellhausen 1885, p. 178]. Japhet agrees that the text is incoherent, and she traces the cause to method: “A strict adherence to the original text and at the same time its adaptation according to various tendencies may result in internal incoherence” [Japhet 1993, p. 362]. She also reports that Rudolph restored a missing passage by conjecture, and she explains why that repair is weak [Japhet 1993, p. 362]. confirmed for the quotations; whether the omission is theological or accidental is disputed.

C. The promise to David (2 Sam 7:16 and 1 Chr 17:14)

In Samuel, David’s own house and kingdom will be secure. In Chronicles the subject changes: “it is not the ‘house’ and ‘kingdom’ of David which ‘shall be established’; rather, Solomon will be confirmed for ever in the ‘house’ and ‘kingdom’ of the Lord” [Japhet 1993, pp. 334–335]. Japhet ties this to the problem that David did not build the Temple, which the Chronicler met in three ways: by enlarging David’s role in preparing the Temple, by softening David’s ideal image, and by stressing that Solomon is also “chosen” [Japhet 1993, p. 335]. Wellhausen read the same verse and found the original meaning “volatilised into an abstract idealism” [Wellhausen 1885, p. 177]. confirmed for the quotations; the interpretation is disputed.

D. Manasseh (2 Kings 21 and 2 Chronicles 33)

The two accounts of Manasseh’s sins (2 Kgs 21:1–9 and 2 Chr 33:1–9) are close in wording. They part at the end: Kings gives the king a short closing notice and burial “in the garden of Uzza,” and Chronicles inserts an Assyrian capture, a prayer, and a return to Jerusalem (33:11–13). Wellhausen: “The Book of Kings knows no worse ruler than Manasseh was; yet he reigned undisturbed for fifty-five years … This is a stone of stumbling that Chronicles must remove” [Wellhausen 1885, pp. 206–207]. Japhet argues that the whole of this period was reworked “to provide … more solid theological cohesiveness,” beginning “in the change of Manasseh’s figure,” and she shows how the change prepares the new account of Josiah [Japhet 1993, pp. 1019, 1034]. confirmed for the quotations; whether the captivity happened is disputed (Part 5).

Hebrew and English for all eight passages in Table 1 were fetched from Sefaria and compared with the verse numbers cited by Japhet and Wellhausen. The 1917 translation renders “moved” where the Hebrew verb is wayyaset (“incited”); Japhet translates it “incited” [Japhet 1993, p. 373].

2.3 The sources the Chronicler names

Samuel and Kings end most reigns with a note such as “the rest of the acts of … are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.” Chronicles keeps the habit but changes the titles. Japhet counts eighteen works cited in the closing formulas: six with general titles (for example “the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel”) and twelve ascribed to prophets (for example “the chronicles of Samuel the seer”), including Samuel, Nathan, Gad, Ahijah, Iddo, Shemaiah, Jehu, Isaiah and Hozai [Japhet 1993, p. 20]. confirmed

Whether these were really eighteen separate books is disputed. Japhet notes that a work with a general title is never cited together with a prophetic work for the same reign, and that two double titles (“the chronicles of Jehu son of Hanani, which are recorded in the Book of the Kings of Israel,” 2 Chr 20:34; “the vision of Isaiah … in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel,” 2 Chr 32:32) show that the prophetic works were “extracts from a comprehensive book” [Japhet 1993, p. 20]. Wellhausen went further. He accepted Ewald’s view that the “Midrash of the Book of Kings” (2 Chr 24:27) is the real title of the source called simply “the Book of Kings,” and concluded that “in Chronicles we find ourselves fully within the period of the scribes” [Wellhausen 1885, p. 227]. [2 Chr 24:27 on Sefaria]

2.4 Which text of Samuel did he copy?

A Vorlage (German for “model” or “source text”) is the exact wording an author or translator worked from. The question is whether the Samuel-Kings in front of the Chronicler matched our Masoretic Text (MT, the medieval Hebrew text). It sometimes did not.

  • Japhet reports that where Chronicles differs from MT Samuel, it sometimes agrees with variant readings of the Septuagint, and that fragments of Samuel from Qumran (4QSama) show matches with Chronicles against MT. She cites W. E. Lemke’s 1965 article (Harvard Theological Review 58, pp. 349–363) and Eugene Ulrich’s study of the Qumran text of Samuel (1978) [Japhet 1993, p. 29] [Lemke 1965]. She concludes that Chronicles reflects “a Vorlage different from the MT” [Japhet 1993, p. 29]. confirmed
  • S. L. McKenzie (1985) pressed the idea further: he argued that the Chronicler’s version of the Deuteronomistic history was not the form we have. Japhet disagrees: she holds that the history was “extant basically in its final canonical form” and that the Chronicler consciously departs from it [Japhet 1993, p. 27] [McKenzie 1985]. disputed
  • Japhet shows how to test a case. The omission of 2 Sam 5:4–5 in 1 Chr 11 was long thought to be the Chronicler’s choice. 4QSama also lacks the verses, which raises the chance that they were missing from his copy. But she finds the same verse (2 Sam 5:5) reused in 1 Chr 3:4 without the phrase “over Judah,” and concludes the omission is the Chronicler’s own work [Japhet 1993, p. 238]. confirmed for her argument; whether she is right is still disputed.

Japhet’s caution on method: “the more familiar we become with the Chronicler’s literary methods, historical views and theology, the more refined our considerations may become” [Japhet 1993, p. 19].

Why it matters

A difference between Chronicles and Kings can mean three different things: the Chronicler changed the text; the Chronicler copied a different text of Samuel-Kings; or the Masoretic Text changed later. Telling these apart is the main skill of the field, and the Qumran scrolls made it possible.

3Part three

German scholarship, 1806–1883

De Wette · his critics · Zunz · Graf and Wellhausen · why Chronicles was the test case · about 20 minutes

Between 1806 and 1883 German-language scholars set the terms in which Chronicles is still discussed. The argument started with one question, whether Chronicles can be trusted as a history of the monarchy. It grew into an argument over the age of the law of Moses. This part follows the argument through ten works (Table 2) and puts each in its institutional and confessional setting. For this part I looked at the books themselves as page images, because machine reading of German Gothic type (Fraktur) is unreliable. Every German or Latin quotation below was checked against a page image. The translations are mine. Where I know a work only through another scholar, the text says so.

Key dates
  1. 1806de Wette’s Beiträge vol. 1: a critical essay on Chronicles as a source for the history of the Mosaic law.
  2. 1819Dahler answers de Wette in Latin at Strasbourg. In the same year de Wette is dismissed from his post in Berlin (not because of Chronicles).
  3. 1823Gramberg sides with de Wette; a thesis by Hengstenberg at Bonn opens with the words “de Wette’s opinion on the Pentateuch is false.”
  4. 1832Zunz: Chronicles and Ezra are one work, written about 260 BCE.
  5. 1833–1834Keil’s “apologetic essay” defends Chronicles; Movers (Catholic, Bonn) dates the book late but defends its use of sources.
  6. 1854Bertheau’s commentary: the one-work view is “almost universally recognized.”
  7. 1866Graf: the traditional view of the law “rests mainly” on Chronicles.
  8. 1878, 1883Wellhausen starts his history of Israel from Chronicles, “where the matter is clearest.”

3.1 The setting: faculties, confessions and what was at stake

Biblical criticism in these years was done mostly in university faculties of theology, and the faculties were tied to churches and states. De Wette began as a lecturer (Privatdozent) at Jena, as his title page says [de Wette 1806, title page]. His career shows what the ties meant. He went to Heidelberg in 1807 and to Berlin in 1810. In 1819 he was dismissed: after the poet Kotzebue was murdered by K. L. Sand, de Wette wrote a letter of consolation to Sand’s mother, and Berlin pietists denounced him to the king. From 1822 he taught at Basel [NDB 1957]. confirmed The same biography says that his liberal theological and political views drew opposition from those pietist circles already, so the dismissal was not about Chronicles.

The scholars in this part belonged to different worlds. Dahler taught at the Protestant seminary of Strasbourg (title page) [Dahler 1819, title page]. Gramberg was a senior teacher at a Prussian school in Züllichau (title page) [Gramberg 1823, title page]. Keil was a young theologian (a licentiate) in Berlin, who thanks Ernst Wilhelm Hengstenberg for help in his preface [Keil 1833, p. XII]. Movers was a Catholic: his book carries the printing permit (imprimatur) of the vicar general of Cologne, dated 21 September 1833 [Movers 1834, imprimatur page], and he later held a chair in the Catholic faculty at Breslau [Ska 2021, p. 27]. Zunz was a Jewish scholar who worked outside the universities. In 1819 he helped found the Society for the Culture and Science of the Jews in Berlin, and he edited its journal [Ska 2021, p. 26]. confirmed

What was at stake

The old view was that Moses wrote the Pentateuch, including the laws on priests, Levites and sacrifice. Chronicles seems to support that view, because it shows David and Solomon arranging the Temple worship by “what is written in the law of Moses.” Samuel and Kings show much less of it. Ska puts the reason for de Wette’s choice of Chronicles in these words: it is the one book that makes the Mosaic law look old, so that to show the book unreliable is to open the way to a later date for the law [Ska 2021, pp. 20–21]. That is Ska’s reading; de Wette’s own words are in 3.2. Graf stated the old view plainly: the traditional Jewish-church view “rests mainly on the Book of Chronicles,” apart from the belief that Moses wrote the whole legislation [Graf 1866, p. 114]. disputed

The stakes were therefore also stakes of belief, and the writers say so. Keil states that he wrote “to defend, in its historically well-founded rights, the authority of a biblical book” that had been attacked by “apparent reasons,” and that, in his belief, no writing by a “bold and calculating deceiver” could have been taken into the canon, which arose “under divine influence” [Keil 1833, pp. IX–X]. Wellhausen answers this attitude in 1883: “Starting from a similar assumption, such an author as C. F. Keil could even at the present day write a book of Chronicles, if this were not already in existence” [Wellhausen 1885, p. 225]. Both statements are in the sources as printed. This part reports them and does not decide between them. confirmed

3.2 De Wette, 1806: the first critical essay on Chronicles

The first volume of de Wette’s Contributions to the Introduction to the Old Testament (Beiträge zur Einleitung in das Alte Testament) has the title Kritischer Versuch über die Glaubwürdigkeit der Bücher der Chronik, “A critical essay on the credibility of the books of Chronicles,” and the subtitle “with regard to the history of the Mosaic books and legislation” (Figure 5). It appeared at Halle in 1806, when de Wette was 26 [de Wette 1806, title page]. The second volume, on the Mosaic history, followed in 1807 [Wellhausen 1883, p. 4, n.]. confirmed A recent survey dates the work 1807 [Ska 2021, p. 20, n. 20]; the title page of volume 1 reads 1806.

The contradiction. De Wette opens by naming a difference in the whole picture of religion, not in single reports [de Wette 1806, p. 4]:

Die Relation der BB. Samuels und der Könige und die der Chronik stehen mit einander in Widerspruch; und zwar nicht bloß in einzelnen Nachrichten (was sich vielleicht leicht übertragen ließe), sondern im Ganzen der Geschichte.The account of the books of Samuel and Kings and that of Chronicles contradict each other; and not only in single reports (which might perhaps be borne easily) but in the whole of the history.[de Wette 1806, p. 4]

The difference he stresses is the history of worship. Chronicles, he says, shows the state of worship from David on as entirely Mosaic-Levitical, with periodic lapses. Samuel and Kings show “little or nothing” of this Levitical ceremonial, but many more neglects and breaches of Levitical laws, and traces of “an unpriestly freedom of worship” [de Wette 1806, pp. 4–5]. He adds that, as far as he knows, no one before him has noticed the contradiction [de Wette 1806, p. 5]. confirmed for the quotations.

The method. De Wette compares the two accounts passage by passage. One of his examples is the bringing of the ark to Jerusalem. In Samuel (2 Sam 6) the Levites are not mentioned; in Chronicles (1 Chr 13–15) David summons them to carry the ark. De Wette asks why, if the Levites were summoned and had the right to carry it, they did not carry it at the first attempt. His answer [de Wette 1806, p. 90]:

Die ursprüngliche Relation sagt nichts von den Leviten, und der Verf. der Chronik konnte sie nur hineinbringen, indem er sein Original entstellte und verstümmelte, und mit sich selbst in Widerspruch gerieth. […] Das Falsum liegt am Tage, so wie die Absicht desselben.The original account says nothing of the Levites, and the author of Chronicles could only bring them in by distorting and cutting his original, and so falling into contradiction with himself. […] The falsification is plain, and so is its purpose.[de Wette 1806, p. 90]

Japhet, in her commentary, singles out another of de Wette’s comparisons, the story of Joash and Jehoiada (2 Chr 23 beside 2 Kgs 11, his pages 91–95; the page in Figure 5 is part of it). She says he chose it first, and Wellhausen after him, as an example of the Chronicler’s method [Japhet 1993, p. 827]. confirmed

A harsh verdict, stated openly. Where de Wette meets a contradiction he does not try to remove, he lets it stand and blames the book: “I leave the contradiction, and put it down to the partiality and spuriousness of Chronicles” [de Wette 1806, p. 132]. Earlier on the same page he asks why one should “take trouble to rescue a credibility that is already lost.” The German reads Warum sollen wir uns hier die Mühe geben, eine Glaubwürdigkeit zu retten, die schon verloren ist? [de Wette 1806, p. 132]. Dahler read this as a charge of bad faith (3.3). confirmed

The date, and what follows for the Pentateuch. De Wette dates the book from the genealogy of Zerubbabel in 1 Chr 3:19–24, which he reads as running down to Alexander’s time: “therefore, we conclude rightly, the Chronicle was written only in Alexander’s time” [de Wette 1806, p. 46]. Then he draws the consequence for the Pentateuch [de Wette 1806, p. 135]:

So wie die ganze Jüdische Geschichte von ihrer interessantesten und wichtigsten Seite, nämlich der der Religion und des gottesdienstlichen Cultus, nach Wegräumung der Nachrichten der Chronik, […] eine ganz andere Gestalt erhält; so erhalten auch die Untersuchungen über den Pentateuch auf einmal eine ganz andere Wendung: eine Menge lästiger, schwer wegzuräumender Beweise für das frühe Vorhandenseyn der Mosaischen Bücher sind verschwunden.Just as the whole of Jewish history, on its most interesting and important side, that of religion and worship, takes on a quite different shape once the reports of Chronicles are cleared away, […] so the investigations of the Pentateuch also take a quite different turn at once: a host of troublesome proofs, hard to remove, for the early existence of the Mosaic books have disappeared.[de Wette 1806, p. 135]

The ellipses mark the long clause in which he says that Chronicles shows early times “through the coloured medium of later Ezraic-Levitical centuries” (durch das gefärbte Medium später Esraisch-levitischer Jahrhunderte). His summary of the whole inquiry: “until Josiah no trace of the existence of the Pentateuch, afterwards, especially after the exile, the most frequent and clearest” [de Wette 1806, p. 182]. Under Josiah, he writes, “all the demands of Deuteronomy are fulfilled” and a book of the law is found, and “everything agrees” on introducing Deuteronomy then [de Wette 1806, p. 299]. confirmed for the quotations; disputed for the conclusions, which later scholars qualified.

Later editions of de Wette’s textbook softened his judgment. Bertheau says he took back “the hard and unfounded judgment” on the credibility of Chronicles in places, “chiefly as a result of the investigations of Movers” [Bertheau 1854, p. XLIX]. confirmed

3.3 The first replies, 1807–1834

Gramberg’s preface of 1823 gives the earliest account I could check of how de Wette was answered. Eichhorn declared against him in a review of 1807 (in the Jena Allgemeine Literatur-Zeitung); Dahler then “repeated and developed what Eichhorn had stated more briefly”; and J. M. Herz, bishop of Ripen, wrote against de Wette in 1822 [Gramberg 1823, p. VI]. I did not open Eichhorn’s review or Herz’s book. confirmed for Gramberg’s report; [unconfirmed] for their contents. The four works I did open were these.

Dahler (1819). A Latin treatise on the authority and historical faith of the books of Chronicles, from a Strasbourg professor. Its first page says no one “has gone further” than de Wette, who accuses the author of bad faith and falsified history; on closer examination, Dahler writes, he was persuaded that nearly all of this “strays far from the truth,” and that the author of Chronicles must be fully acquitted [Dahler 1819, p. 1]. The Latin is auctorem Chronicorum ab ista culpa plane absolvendum. I read no further than this page and the dedication. confirmed for the page; [unconfirmed] for the argument.

Gramberg (1823). His book is often listed among the replies to de Wette, but his preface says the opposite. He sets out to justify “the result that Messrs. Gesenius and de Wette have given,” with modifications, and “especially to defend it against Professor Dahler” [Gramberg 1823, p. VII]. He adds that Dahler ignores the grammatical work of Gesenius (the language of Chronicles is late) [Gramberg 1823, p. VI]. confirmed for the preface. A survey of 2021 puts Gramberg among the authors who “attacked de Wette directly” [Ska 2021, p. 25, n. 33]; the preface shows that this is an error (see the list of corrections). I did not read Gramberg’s chapters. Bertheau, who did, calls them rarely useful, with “arbitrary and rash assertions” [Bertheau 1854, p. XLIX].

Keil (1833). A young Berlin theologian wrote the “apologetic essay” on Chronicles and on the integrity of Ezra. “A longer and more careful examination of the doubts raised in recent times against the credibility of the books of Chronicles led the author to the conviction that they are untenable.” He found in them “less the pure interest in truth than certain unhistorical prejudices” [Keil 1833, p. IX]. The German is gewisse unhistorische Vorurtheile. His preface is dated Berlin, 6 January 1833, and thanks Hengstenberg for oral advice and for books [Keil 1833, p. XII]. Ska reports that Hengstenberg’s own thesis at Bonn in 1823 began, Falsa est de Wettii de Pentateucho sententia, “de Wette’s opinion on the Pentateuch is false” [Ska 2021, p. 25]; I know that thesis only through her. confirmed for Keil’s preface.

Movers (1834). A Catholic scholar at Bonn gave the most careful reply. He grants that in the passages that Chronicles shares with the older books, “Chronicles bears the character of a copy; the older work has all the merits of the original” [Movers 1834, p. 9]. But for the history of Israel the book is “of inestimable value,” above all for “church antiquities and institutions” on which Samuel and Kings tell little [Movers 1834, p. 9]. He dates it “at the earliest toward the end of the Persian period, or even beyond, in the time of Alexander or his first successors” [Movers 1834, pp. 10–11]. So Movers granted the late date and still defended the use of sources. Wellhausen thought this a mistake: “many a theological Sisyphus has toiled to roll the stone again wholly or half-way up the hill—Movers especially” [Wellhausen 1885, p. 222]; the German is on p. 231 [Wellhausen 1883, p. 231]. Wellhausen’s complaint is that Movers “mixed up” the question of the book’s historical value with the question of its probable sources, which de Wette had refused to do [Wellhausen 1885, p. 222]. confirmed disputed on how far the sources save the book.

Movers also settled a side question that connects with Part 2.3. The many source titles of Chronicles (“Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah,” and the like) are, in the words of Wellhausen, shown “after Movers” by Bertheau and others to name always one and the same book [Wellhausen 1883, p. 235]. confirmed on Wellhausen’s report; I did not open Movers’s pages on the point.

3.4 Zunz, Ewald and Bertheau: one work

While Dahler and de Wette quarreled over reliability, Zunz was asking a different question: who wrote Chronicles, and when? His book of 1832 is about the history of Jewish preaching, and Chronicles has a chapter of its own (pp. 12–35), followed by a chapter on midrash [Zunz 1832, pp. 12, 35]. Its title promises “a contribution to the knowledge of antiquity and to biblical criticism.” (Midrash: interpretation and retelling of an older text, here used of the Chronicler’s method.)

One work. The two books share their opening and closing lines (Table 4), and many passages in Ezra and Nehemiah are not by Ezra [Zunz 1832, p. 20]. Zunz resolves the problem in a sentence [Zunz 1832, p. 21]:

Diesen gordischen Knoten aber löst der eine Ausspruch: dass wir die Chronik und das Buch Esra als zwei zusammengehörige Theile eines und desselben Werkes ansehen.This Gordian knot is cut by one statement: that we regard Chronicles and the book of Ezra as two connected parts of one and the same work.[Zunz 1832, p. 21]

He then lists what the two share: reports of popular assemblies and festivals, “praises of the Levites and above all of the singers,” “extraordinary care for the sacrificial orders,” a love of genealogies, “exaggerations in numbers,” quotations from the Pentateuch and Psalms, “historical ignorance,” and an “embellishing style” [Zunz 1832, p. 21]. So Zunz did not defend the book’s facts: his list includes “historical ignorance” and exaggeration. confirmed

Date and method. The start of the Seleucid era, 312 BCE, is for Zunz “undoubtedly the furthest limit” for the Chronicler, who is older than the Maccabees (Hanukkah is unknown to him), and the middle date he gives is “the year 260 before Christ” [Zunz 1832, pp. 32–33]. The work was written, he says, “in the post-prophetic age, when law and prophets were long known and revered as the heritage of the past” [Zunz 1832, p. 33]. In the midrash chapter he describes how the Chronicler read the past: he works “for conscious purposes, yet in a spirit of constant subordination,” and tries to read the concepts and interests of the present out of the facts and words of the ancestors. “One adorned the history, which already itself offered legends, with new legends” [Zunz 1832, p. 35]. That is a description of method, not a verdict on reliability. Japhet notes that Zunz tied this midrashic activity to the Great Assembly, and that Wellhausen later used the same word for Chronicles [Japhet 1993, p. 31]. confirmed for the quotations; disputed for the date.

Zunz’s reception is not clear to me. Bertheau gives him credit for the one-work view [Bertheau 1854, p. XXIII], and Ewald confirms it in a footnote. But a text search of the machine-read 1883 Wellhausen finds no mention of Zunz, and I have not read every page [unconfirmed].

Ewald and Bertheau. Heinrich Ewald (Göttingen) reached the same view alone. Chronicles and “the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, which, as I shall soon show, originally belonged to it” form one work (p. 246). A footnote credits Zunz and says that Ewald “noticed only now”, at a new edition, that his own earlier studies had led him to the same result “without my knowing the views of that work” [Ewald 1864, p. 246]. Ewald puts the writing “in the last times of Persian rule, at the most in the first years of Greek rule” [Ewald 1864, p. 249]. Bertheau’s commentary of 1854 says that “in recent times the unity of Chronicles and the book of Ezra (without Nehemiah) is almost universally recognized” [Bertheau 1854, p. XXII]. So by 1854 the one-work view was standard, which is the point made in the box at the start of this seminar. confirmed

3.5 Graf and Wellhausen: why Chronicles became the test case

Graf’s book of 1866 returns to de Wette. Its preface complains that the Book of Chronicles “is placed, without stricter examination, on the same level as the Books of Samuel and Kings as a source of history” [Graf 1866, p. VII]. Its second essay, “The Book of Chronicles as a Source,” opens by saying that the traditional view rests “mainly on the Book of Chronicles,” in which “the historical outlook of the Jewish community in Jerusalem in the second half of the fourth century” speaks [Graf 1866, p. 114]. He criticizes Ewald, Bertheau and Movers (p. 114 and following). confirmed

Wellhausen tells how he came to the view. In 1867 he learned from Ritschl in Göttingen that Graf placed the law after the prophets, and “I was able to admit to myself that Hebrew antiquity could be understood without the book of the Torah” [Wellhausen 1883, p. 4]. He traces “all these men” back to “Martin Lebrecht de Wette, the epoch-making opener of historical criticism in this field,” and cites volume 1 of the Beiträge [Wellhausen 1883, p. 4]. In the 1883 preface he says that the Graf hypothesis “has been put on the order of the day” in Germany and that since 1878 hardly a Hebrew scholar or theologian has failed to take a position on it [Wellhausen 1883, p. III]. confirmed

His chapter “Chronicles” opens with this decision about where to start [Wellhausen 1883, p. 177]:

Wo die Sache am klarsten liegt, setzt die Untersuchung ein, nämlich bei der Chronik. Die Chronik, mit den Büchern Esra und Nehemia eigentlich zusammengehörig, geht im Stoff vollkommen den Büchern Samuelis und der Könige parallel, und wir sind hier in der günstigen Lage, die Vergleichungsobjecte nicht erst wie gewöhnlich durch Quellenscheidung gewinnen zu müssen […] Was aber mehr ist, wir können sie auch ziemlich sicher datieren.We begin the inquiry where the matter is clearest—namely, with the Book of Chronicles. Chronicles, which properly speaking forms but a single book along with Ezra and Nehemiah, is a second history running parallel with the Books of Samuel and Kings, and we are here in the favourable position of starting with the objects of comparison distinctly defined, instead of having as usual to begin by a critical separation of sources […] And, what is more, we can also date the rival histories with tolerable certainty.[Wellhausen 1883, p. 177] [Wellhausen 1885, p. 171]

On the next page he names his debt: “I rely throughout on de Wette’s critical essay on the credibility of the books of Chronicles (Beiträge I, 1806); this treatise has not been improved by Graf” [Wellhausen 1883, p. 178]. The Priestly Code (the part of the Pentateuch with the laws on priests and ritual) is, he says, the cause of the difference: “the difference rests on the influence, which had meanwhile set in, of the Priestly Code” [Wellhausen 1883, p. 178]. For the Chronicler’s past, he coins the line [Wellhausen 1883, p. 233]:

Nicht weil das Gesetz und die Hierokratie […] in der Überlieferung vorgefunden, sondern weil sie darin vermisst wurden, setzte man sie zu.It was not because tradition gave the Law and the hierocracy […] but because these elements were felt to be missing, that they were thus introduced.[Wellhausen 1883, p. 233] [Wellhausen 1885, p. 223]

He calls this “the Judaizing of the past” (die Judaisierung der Vergangenheit) [Wellhausen 1883, p. 233]. On the Chronicler’s style he writes the line that Ska’s survey quotes: Wie Efeu umgrünt derselbe den abgestorbenen Stamm mit fremdartigem Leben, “like ivy it overspreads the dead trunk with extraneous life,” of midrash [Wellhausen 1883, p. 237] [Wellhausen 1885, p. 227]. He does not trace the book to one man’s whim: “It must be admitted that Chronicles owes its origin not to the arbitrariness of an individual, but to a general tendency of the age” [Wellhausen 1883, p. 234] [Wellhausen 1885, p. 225]. confirmed

Why Chronicles became the test case. The sources give four reasons, each of them a step in one chain:

  1. Two accounts of one period. Chronicles covers the same time as Samuel and Kings, so that the two can be compared without first having to separate layers (Wellhausen, p. 177) [Wellhausen 1883, p. 177].
  2. A datable second account. Chronicles can be dated “with tolerable certainty” to well after the Persian empire (Wellhausen, p. 177), or to the fourth century (Graf), or the third (Zunz), and in any case late.
  3. A different picture of worship. De Wette found the Levitical order in Chronicles and little of it in Samuel and Kings (pp. 4–5); Wellhausen explains the difference by the later date, since the Priestly Code had come between [Wellhausen 1883, p. 178].
  4. The consequence for the law. If Chronicles is a reliable witness to David’s age, the Levitical law is old. If it is not, “a host of troublesome proofs” for the early law disappear (de Wette, p. 135), and the tradition on which the old view rests is, in Graf’s words, mainly Chronicles (Graf, p. 114).

Each step has been questioned since. Japhet’s arguments in Part 4 separate the Chronicler’s use of sources from his reliability and from his theology: they are, in her words, “different considerations” [Japhet 1993, p. 18]. She also holds that no single narrow aim, such as an answer to the Priestly Code, explains the whole book [Japhet 1993, p. 43]. disputed

The picture is of a debate in which the main answers came from people in different positions: Protestant lecturers and school teachers, a Catholic professor, a Jewish scholar outside the universities, and Ewald, who was at Göttingen. They did not split cleanly along confessional lines. Gramberg, a Protestant, sided with de Wette. Movers, a Catholic, granted de Wette the late date. Zunz, a Jew, joined the critics on the date but not on the use of the sources. Only Keil and, from what Gramberg and Ska report, Dahler and Hengstenberg wrote openly to defend the authority of the book. disputed

3.6 The long answer: from the “Sisyphus” of Wellhausen to Japhet

For about a century after Wellhausen the verdict stayed: late, partial, unreliable (Part 6.3). Ska opens her survey of 2021 by quoting John Kleinig (1994): “That Cinderella of the Hebrew Bible, Chronicles, has at last emerged from years of obscurity and scorn” [Ska 2021, p. 15]. Three things changed in the twentieth century, and each ties to a part of this seminar.

  • Authorship. By Noth’s time (1943) the one-work view of Zunz and Movers was standard; Japhet’s article of 1968 reopened it [Japhet 1993, pp. 3–4]. This is the dispute in Part 5.1, and the reason Table 4 sets the end of Chronicles beside the start of Ezra.
  • Sources and reliability. Japhet separates the question of sources from the question of reliability and from theology [Japhet 1993, p. 18]. This bears on the quarrel with Movers (3.3), whom Wellhausen accused of mixing the two questions together. Part 5.3 tests the question on three cases.
  • Purpose. De Wette, Zunz and Wellhausen read the differences between Chronicles and Kings as signs of unreliability or of midrash. From Willi’s Chronicles as Interpretation (1972) and Japhet’s Ideology they were read as the Chronicler’s own message [Willi 1972] [Japhet, Ideology]. This is Part 4, argument 3.

The nineteenth-century story has been told at length by others. Ska lists Dietmar Mathias, Die Geschichte der Chronikforschung im 19. Jahrhundert (Leipzig dissertation, 1977), Kai Peltonen, History Debated (1996), and Japhet’s own article on the history of the problem (1985) [Ska 2021, p. 15, n. 1]. I have not opened these three.

Why it matters

Chronicles tells the same centuries as Samuel and Kings but from a later point of view, and it shows a fuller worship. A historian could therefore set two accounts of the same period side by side, and the later one could be dated. If the later account is a retelling, the law it assumes is probably also later. That is why a book that is now read for its theology once carried the whole debate over the age of the Pentateuch.

4.3 Her main arguments

The commentary of 1993 holds her mature view in one place. Quotations below are from its Introduction, by the printed page numbers.

1. Two books, two authors

“Chronicles and Ezra-Nehemiah constitute two different works by two different authors. Not only do they illustrate an array of small and large differences — in language, style, literary method, etc. — and express different and often opposite views about central issues of biblical history and theology, but when considered in their totality they represent two varieties of biblical historical writing during the Persian-Hellenistic period” [Japhet 1993, p. 4]. confirmed for the quotation; the conclusion is disputed. Gunneweg, Haran, Blenkinsopp, Ackroyd and Pohlmann restated the older view in new forms [Japhet 1993, pp. 3–4].

2. One book, one author

Against the many attempts to cut Chronicles into layers (Part 5), she holds that “it is one work, composed essentially by a single author, with a very distinct and peculiar literary method.” She allows later changes “in particular in the lists, which are most susceptible to change,” and doubts that “a rational, meticulous harmony of all the possible details was ever aimed at by the Chronicler” [Japhet 1993, p. 7]. confirmed for the quotations; disputed as a position.

3. No single narrow purpose

Wellhausen, Torrey, Noth, Rudolph and Freedman each found one aim: to answer the Priestly Code, to fight the Samaritans, or to support the house of David under Zerubbabel [Japhet 1993, p. 43]. Japhet doubts that one aim could explain “such an enormous enterprise.” In her words, Chronicles “is not a manifesto devoted to a specific political movement but a more general and comprehensive theological stock-taking, striving to achieve a new religious balance in the face of a changing world” [Japhet 1993, pp. 43–44]. confirmed for the quotation; disputed as a position.

4. Justice that is immediate and individual

The book’s “theory of ‘reward and punishment’” shows history as “a concrete manifestation of divine justice.” In her summary: “Reward is mandatory, immediate and individual. Every generation is requited for its own deeds, both good and evil, with no postponement of recompense; there is no accumulated sin and no accumulated merit.” Two things attend this: warning and repentance. “Man is always offered a chance to repent” [Japhet 1993, pp. 44–45]. The Manasseh story (Part 2, case D) is her example of how the Chronicler adjusted older history to fit this rule [Japhet 1993, p. 1019]. confirmed for the quotations.

5. “Great Israel,” the land and the king

She finds a view of “‘great Israel’ in the broadest sense,” settled across the whole land from the beginning, with “no Gentiles in the land of Israel” in the Chronicler’s picture; the exodus and the exile are “muted” [Japhet 1993, pp. 46–47]. David and Solomon appear “in a much more positive light than in earlier biblical historiography,” yet “neither of them can be considered perfect or ‘ideal’” [Japhet 1993, p. 48]. confirmed for the quotations.

6. Lists as proof

The many lists give the account “the validity and authority of ‘accurate fact’.” A modern reader “may find some lists more authentic than others,” but that does not change their literary job [Japhet 1993, p. 41]. Her caution on sources: even if sources existed, “even authentic sources may be used in an uncritical or anachronistic manner,” so reliability must be judged “on a case-by-case basis” [Japhet 1993, pp. 18–19]. confirmed for the quotations.

7. The date

Japhet puts the book “at the end of the fourth century BCE.” Her grounds: the language is Late Biblical Hebrew; there is no sign of Greek influence; and the Persian administrative system of Ezra–Nehemiah is missing, which may point to a non-Persian setting [Japhet 1993, pp. 25–26]. Her count from the line of Jehoiachin (1 Chr 3:17–24) gives a window of roughly 460–320 BCE, though she calls that method “problematical” [Japhet 1993, p. 26]. See Figure 11. disputed

Why it matters

Japhet changed the question. Earlier scholars asked what older documents lay beneath Chronicles and what political cause it served. She asked what the book itself is: one work with its own method, its own view of history and its own place beside Ezra–Nehemiah. Even readers who reject her answers now have to argue with them.

5Part five

The debates

Authorship · date · how far Chronicles is history · about 25 minutes

Chronicles has been read in three main ways over 150 years: as late and unreliable history (Wellhausen), as a work with many hands (Noth and others), and as one author’s unified answer to his times (Japhet and many later writers). This part follows the three disputes in turn: who wrote it, when, and how far it can be trusted.

5.1 Authorship and layers

Two questions are tangled together. The first: did one person write Chronicles and also Ezra–Nehemiah? The tradition said yes, and said that person was Ezra the scribe (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 15a; also John of Salisbury and Ralph Niger in the Middle Ages) [Japhet 1993, p. 3]. Zunz (1832) and Movers (1834) kept the idea of one author but dropped Ezra and called him “the Chronicler”; their view “eventually gained general recognition” [Japhet 1993, p. 3]. confirmed Albright alone, among modern scholars, went back to Ezra himself [Japhet 1993, p. 24]. confirmed After 1968 the view of two independent works spread [Japhet 1993, p. 4].

The second question is whether the book as we have it is the original. Its mix of narrative and long lists, of priestly and Deuteronomistic features, led many to see layers. Japhet sorts the attempts into four groups: “source” theories (Kittel, Benzinger); the removal of whole sections such as the lists (Welch); tradition-history with “wild growth” around a core close to the Deuteronomistic history (Noth, Rudolph, Willi); and staged composition (Galling; Cross, with three stages from the sixth to the fourth century) [Japhet 1993, pp. 5–6]. Her own verdict: “each of these approaches has come with its own, idiosyncratic ‘Chronicler’” [Japhet 1993, p. 7]. confirmed for what she says; the disputes themselves are disputed.

Cross and Freedman: a political reading

Freedman (1961) and Cross (1975), with others, tied the book to the time of Zerubbabel, the leader from the house of David in the late sixth century [Japhet 1993, pp. 7, 25] [Cross 1975]. Freedman argued that its purpose was to support the claims of the house of David to rule, and in particular its claim to authority over the Temple and its worship [Japhet 1993, p. 43]. Japhet doubts that any single political aim fits the book (Part 4, argument 3). disputed

5.2 The date

Nothing in Chronicles names an event of its own time, so every date is an inference. Japhet lists the clues [Japhet 1993, pp. 24–26]:

  • The Hebrew is Late Biblical Hebrew: not earlier than the post-exilic age.
  • No Greek influence is visible, which suggests a time before the strong Hellenistic influence of the third century BCE.
  • The line of Jehoiachin in 1 Chr 3:17–24 reaches “between seven and fourteen generations” after him, depending on how the damaged list is read; at about twenty years a generation this gives a wide window.

Wellhausen placed Chronicles “fully three hundred years” after the Books of Samuel and Kings, “after the downfall of the Persian empire” [Wellhausen 1885, p. 172]. A recent commentator, Knoppers, reaches “around the mid third century BCE,” by allowing time both for Chronicles to be quoted by later writers and for its own sources to become authoritative, as reported by one reviewer [ABR review of Knoppers]. disputed: I did not read Knoppers myself, so the figure rests on the review [unconfirmed]. Japhet’s own text says the most common view puts the book in the fourth century or toward its end, and that the full range of proposals spans over four hundred years [Japhet 1993, p. 24]. confirmed

Why it matters

The date decides what the book is evidence for. Written around 400 BCE, it speaks about the Persian province of Judah. Written in the third century, it speaks about a community already under Hellenistic rule. Either way it is a witness to its own age first, and to the age of David second.

5.3 How far is Chronicles history?

Japhet separates two questions that older scholars joined: whether the Chronicler had sources, and whether his book is reliable. She holds that he did use sources beyond Samuel and Kings, because “the analysis of Chronicles as a literary work seems to leave no doubt” of it, and that this still does not settle reliability: “even the existence of ‘sources’ does not guarantee the reliability of the book” [Japhet 1993, p. 18]. Even Wellhausen granted non-synoptic sources [Japhet 1993, p. 19]. confirmed

Wellhausen’s own verdict was harsher. Of the long list of David’s supporters in 1 Chr 12 he wrote that the “vast numbers … are not matters of indifference here, but the principal thing,” and he called the whole picture “hardly credible” [Wellhausen 1885, pp. 174–175]. Japhet’s answer is about purpose, not accuracy: lists serve to bolster the account with “accurate fact” [Japhet 1993, p. 41]. Both are disputed as readings. Three test cases follow.

Case 1. Hezekiah’s tunnel

Kings and Chronicles both mention Hezekiah’s water works, with different words (Table 3). Kings speaks of the pool, the conduit and bringing water “into the city.” Chronicles says he “stopped the upper spring of the waters of Gihon” and brought them “straight down on the west side of the city of David” [2 Kgs 20:20 on Sefaria] [2 Chr 32:30 on Sefaria].

Table 3. Hezekiah’s water works in Kings and in Chronicles. Hebrew: Sefaria; English: JPS 1917.

2 Kings 20:202 Chronicles 32:30
2 Kings 20:20

וְיֶתֶר דִּבְרֵי חִזְקִיָּהוּ וְכׇל־גְּבוּרָתוֹ וַאֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה אֶת־הַבְּרֵכָה וְאֶת־הַתְּעָלָה וַיָּבֵא אֶת־הַמַּיִם הָעִירָה הֲלֹא־הֵם כְּתוּבִים עַל־סֵפֶר דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים לְמַלְכֵי יְהוּדָה׃

Now the rest of the acts of Hezekiah, and all his might, and how he made the pool, and the conduit, and brought water into the city, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?

2 Chronicles 32:30

וְהוּא יְחִזְקִיָּהוּ סָתַם אֶת־מוֹצָא מֵימֵי גִיחוֹן הָעֶלְיוֹן וַיַּישְּׁרֵם לְמַטָּה־מַּעְרָבָה לְעִיר דָּוִיד וַיַּצְלַח יְחִזְקִיָּהוּ בְּכׇל־מַעֲשֵׂהוּ׃

This same Hezekiah also stopped the upper spring of the waters of Gihon, and brought them straight down on the west side of the city of David. And Hezekiah prospered in all his works.

  • The Siloam Tunnel is 533 meters long. It is usually called Hezekiah’s Tunnel, and, according to Maeir and Chadwick, most scholars accept it as part of his preparations before the Assyrian attack of 701 BCE [Maeir and Chadwick 2013].
  • In 2003 Frumkin, Shimron and Rosenbaum reported radiocarbon and uranium–thorium dates that, they wrote, prove an Iron Age II date and show that “the Biblical text presents an accurate historic record” of the tunnel’s construction [Frumkin et al. 2003]. disputed: this is their conclusion, and the abstract is all I read.
  • Other studies disagree. Sneh, Shalev and Weinberger (2010) argue that the tunnel is later and was cut by Manasseh; they read 2 Chr 32:30 as pointing to a different channel, the Siloam Channel. Reich and Shukron (2011) argue that the tunnel was dug before Hezekiah. Maeir and Chadwick criticize the first view: Isaiah 7:3 and 8:6 point to the older channel being in use before Hezekiah, and Hezekiah’s revolt left four years for the work (705 to 701 BCE) [Maeir and Chadwick 2013]. disputed
  • No inscription names Hezekiah as the builder [Maeir and Chadwick 2013]. The tunnel therefore tests the verse; the verse does not prove the date.

Case 2. Manasseh in Assyrian records

Kings gives Manasseh a short closing notice; Chronicles adds a capture, a prayer, and a return (2 Chr 33:11–13; Table 1, part D). The Assyrian text called Esarhaddon’s Prism B lists “Manasseh, king of Judah” among twelve rulers of the Levant who were called on, in 676/675 BCE, to send building materials for a monument at Nineveh [Esarhaddon Prism B]. That is the only Assyrian mention of him I opened, and it says nothing about a captivity, for or against. A silence of this kind is weak evidence; the prism is a list of contributions. disputed Japhet argues from the book’s theology, not from outside records: the story of Manasseh’s repentance fits the rule that every generation is paid for its own deeds, and it prepares the new Josiah story [Japhet 1993, pp. 1019, 1034]. I did not find a source that settles the question.

Case 3. Yehud: how big and how populous?

Yehud is the Aramaic name for Judah as a province of the Persian empire. The genealogies and lists of Chronicles have been used as a map of the province, so its size matters. Finkelstein (2010) argues that the distribution of stamped jar handles with the name Yehud covers only the area around Jerusalem (between Ramat Rahel and the City of David), with some finds at Jericho and En-Gedi. The list of wall builders in Nehemiah 3, in his view, does not fit Persian-period archaeology, and he suggests it may reflect the Hasmonean period of the second century BCE. From site sizes he estimates about 61 built-up hectares and “ca. 12,000 people” for the whole province, about half the figure of Carter and Lipschits (20,000 to 30,000), and a few hundred in Jerusalem itself [Finkelstein 2010]. disputed: Finkelstein’s numbers rest on a density assumption of 200 persons per built-up hectare, which he sets lower than other scholars do. estimate

For Chronicles the result is two-sided. On one hand, a small province is hard to square with the “great Israel” of the genealogies. On the other, Finkelstein says that the genealogies of Judah and Benjamin “cannot help reconstructing the ‘territoriality’ of Yehud,” as J. W. Wright had tried to do in 2006, because “they may represent post-Persian-period realities” [Finkelstein 2010, n. 27]. disputed

Another test: the capture of Jerusalem

Kalimi (2005), as summarized by his reviewer, concludes that Chronicles “does not contain authentic data about the capture of Jerusalem”: it leaves out the earlier attempts at the city, and adds “all Israel” in 1 Chr 11:4 against 2 Sam 5:6. Its aim is to mark a new epoch with David’s reign [ABR review of Kalimi]. disputed: I know this only from the review.
