Why it matters

The disputes are not signs of a weak field. Each answer changes what the book can be used for: as evidence of what happened under the kings, as evidence of what the Persian-age community believed, or both. Learn to ask, for any claim about Chronicles, which of those two uses it assumes.

6Part six

Why it matters

A rewritten past · the Second Temple setting · reception · about 15 minutes

6.1 A history rewritten, on purpose

Chronicles “constitutes a comprehensive parallel to the earlier biblical historiography from Genesis to Kings” and ends “pointing toward a new era” [Japhet 1993, p. 8]. It is not a copy. The Chronicler used Samuel and Kings “as his point of departure,” and reworked them “through omissions, additions, rephrasing and epitomization” [Japhet 1993, p. 976]. Three results are worth keeping in mind.

  • A different David. The Bathsheba story is gone, David’s sins are reduced to two, and he is ruled out of building the Temple because “he shed blood” [Japhet 1993, p. 48]. His son Solomon is “flawless” [Japhet 1993, p. 48]. confirmed
  • A different Josiah. In Kings the great reform begins in his eighteenth year, after the book of the Law is found. In Chronicles “Josiah did not wait until the eighteenth year of his reign. The change of disposition occurred in the eighth year of his reign ‘while he was yet a boy’ (34.3)”; the reform cleans the land, not the Temple, and the finding of the book comes by chance during repairs [Japhet 1993, pp. 1019–1020]. Japhet explains these changes as answers to theological problems in the older account: Josiah is praised lavishly in Kings, yet in that account he ruled seventeen years amid idolatry unpunished [Japhet 1993, p. 1019]; and the judgment on Judah stays fixed whatever Josiah did, which leaves “no possibility of repentance” [Japhet 1993, p. 1034]. confirmed for the quotations.
  • Continuity with the Temple. Kalimi (2005), as summarized by his reviewer, argues that the Chronicler stresses continuity between the First and Second Temples. He follows the tradition in Jeremiah 27–28 and Ezra that the Temple vessels were kept by the Babylonians, where 2 Kings 24:13 says they were destroyed [ABR review of Kalimi]. disputed: I know this only from the review.

6.2 The Second Temple setting

The world behind the book is the Persian empire and, after it, the Hellenistic kingdoms. In that world Judah was a small province. Figure 14 shows the empire; Figure 16 shows a coin of the province itself.

The book ends with a decree of Cyrus. The clay cylinder in Figure 15 is the best-known royal text of his reign. The British Museum’s account says it was “written from a purely Babylonian point of view,” that Cyrus appears in it as the chosen servant of Marduk, and that it records the return of deported peoples and their gods to their cities. The same entry states that the cylinder “says nothing of human rights” (against a popular label), and that “the return of the Jews and of other deported peoples was a significant reversal of the policies of earlier Assyrian and Babylonian kings” [British Museum]. The museum’s list of names in the inscription has no Jerusalem and no Judah. The cylinder therefore matches the kind of policy that Ezra and Chronicles attribute to Cyrus, and it does not confirm the edict as the Bible words it. confirmed for what the museum says; disputed for how much the cylinder supports the biblical edict.

Table 4. The edict of Cyrus, as Chronicles ends and as Ezra begins. The two texts are the same through “which is in Judah” and then divide. Differences and kept clauses are marked.

2 Chronicles 36:22–23 (the end of the book)Ezra 1:1–3 (the same edict, continued)
2 Chronicles 36:22–23

וּבִשְׁנַת אַחַת לְכוֹרֶשׁ מֶלֶךְ פָּרַס לִכְלוֹת דְּבַר־יְהֹוָה בְּפִי יִרְמְיָהוּ הֵעִיר יְהֹוָה אֶת־רוּחַ כּוֹרֶשׁ מֶלֶךְ־פָּרַס וַיַּעֲבֶר־קוֹל בְּכׇל־מַלְכוּתוֹ וְגַם־בְּמִכְתָּב לֵאמֹר׃ כֹּה־אָמַר כּוֹרֶשׁ מֶלֶךְ פָּרַס כׇּל־מַמְלְכוֹת הָאָרֶץ נָתַן לִי יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵי הַשָּׁמַיִם וְהוּא־פָקַד עָלַי לִבְנוֹת־לוֹ בַיִת בִּירוּשָׁלִַם אֲשֶׁר בִּיהוּדָה מִי־בָכֶם מִכׇּל־עַמּוֹ יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהָיו עִמּוֹ וְיָעַל׃

Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be accomplished, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom, and put it also in writing, saying: ’Thus saith Cyrus king of Persia: All the kingdoms of the earth hath the LORD, the God of heaven, given me; and He hath charged me to build Him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Whosoever there is among you of all His people—the LORD his God be with him—let him go up.’

Ezra 1:1–3

וּבִשְׁנַת אַחַת לְכוֹרֶשׁ מֶלֶךְ פָּרַס לִכְלוֹת דְּבַר־יְהֹוָה מִפִּי יִרְמְיָה הֵעִיר יְהֹוָה אֶת־רוּחַ כֹּרֶשׁ מֶלֶךְ־פָּרַס וַיַּעֲבֶר־קוֹל בְּכׇל־מַלְכוּתוֹ וְגַם־בְּמִכְתָּב לֵאמֹר׃ כֹּה אָמַר כֹּרֶשׁ מֶלֶךְ פָּרַס כֹּל מַמְלְכוֹת הָאָרֶץ נָתַן לִי יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵי הַשָּׁמָיִם וְהוּא־פָקַד עָלַי לִבְנוֹת־לוֹ בַיִת בִּירוּשָׁלִַם אֲשֶׁר בִּיהוּדָה׃ מִי־בָכֶם מִכׇּל־עַמּוֹ יְהִי אֱלֹהָיו עִמּוֹ וְיַעַל לִירוּשָׁלִַם אֲשֶׁר בִּיהוּדָה וְיִבֶן אֶת־בֵּית יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא הָאֱלֹהִים אֲשֶׁר בִּירוּשָׁלִָם׃

NOW IN the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be accomplished, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom, and put it also in writing, saying: ’Thus saith Cyrus king of Persia: All the kingdoms of the earth hath the LORD, the God of heaven, given me; and He hath charged me to build Him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Whosoever there is among you of all His people—his God be with him—let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel, He is the God who is in Jerusalem.

Chronicles stops at “let him go up” (Hebrew וְיָעַל, we-ya‘al); Ezra goes on, “to Jerusalem … and build the house of the LORD.” Kalimi reads the cut as deliberate, a call to more exiles to return, since the last word of Chronicles is “go up” [ABR review of Kalimi]. Others see an ordinary ending of the book. disputed: Japhet notes only that the edict is one of two passages Chronicles takes from Ezra–Nehemiah [Japhet 1993, p. 27]. The point for the seminar is the reuse itself: the book that retells the monarchy ends on a text from the Persian age and from another biblical book. This is also why the question of common authorship (Part 5) matters.

Money confirms that the province had its own identity. Finkelstein notes the “high level of silver” in the Yehud coins and links it with their role in the Temple economy, but he says this only “seemingly” [Finkelstein 2010]. disputed

Why it matters

Chronicles belongs to the age of the Second Temple. It shows no trace of the Persian administrative system (Japhet, p. 26), yet its themes (a central Temple, a Levitical order, one people in one land, justice in each generation) answer the needs of a small community led from Jerusalem under a distant empire. To read it is to see how that community told its own past.

6.3 How the book was received

In Jewish tradition

  • It was counted as part of the canon from early times. Josephus’s “thirteen books” of prophetic history “must have included Chronicles” (Japhet’s inference), and the rabbis list it among the Writings [Japhet 1993, pp. 1–2]. confirmed
  • It was studied less than other books. Walfish writes that “Chronicles has not traditionally been a very popular book for Jews to study,” that “there is no midrashic compilation on Chronicles,” and that there are only nineteen extant medieval commentaries up to the end of the eighteenth century, “a very low figure” [Walfish 2012, pp. 101–102]. confirmed
  • Yet it was never ignored. Walfish also says that Kalimi shows it “was never totally neglected,” and that a circle of scholars in twelfth-century Germany took a particular interest in it; one anonymous commentary of that school, long attributed to Rashi, is dated by Viezel to 1155 [Walfish 2012, pp. 103–104, 106]. Radak (David Kimhi), a grammarian and exegete of Provence, wrote one of the best-known commentaries [Walfish 2012, p. 102]. confirmed
  • Spinoza (1670), in a passage Walfish quotes, wrote that he had “always been astonished” that certain books were included in the Bible while others were excluded, and added “it is not my intention to detract from their authority.” Walfish reads the passage as about Chronicles and says Spinoza “distinctly states that he is not out to question the book’s authority” [Walfish 2012, p. 104].

In Christian tradition

  • The Septuagint (Greek) title Paraleipomena, “things left over,” “may carry negative connotations,” and some Syriac fathers wanted the book removed from scripture; “except for these late voices … the canonicity of Chronicles is firmly established in all traditions” [Japhet 1993, p. 1]. confirmed
  • The Septuagint and Vulgate place it after Kings, an order that “influenced its position in many modern translations” [Japhet 1993, p. 2]. In the Middle Ages Christian writers such as John of Salisbury and Ralph Niger, and Stephen Langton (who wrote a commentary on Chronicles), took it as the work of Ezra [Japhet 1993, pp. 3, 24]. confirmed
  • The claim that Chronicles was “neglected” by Christian readers as a rule: no source I opened shows it. The sources show doubts in one Syriac school and a late rise of critical doubt, not general neglect. unsupported

In modern research

Wellhausen’s verdict set the tone for a century: late, partial, unreliable. From the 1960s onward the book’s own method and message came to the front (Freedman, Willi, Williamson, Japhet). Japhet’s Ideology is credited by its publisher with being “recognized as a major distillation of the themes underlying the ideology of the book of Chronicles” [Japhet, Ideology]. confirmed for the quotation; the judgment is the publisher’s.

Key dates
  1. End of the narrativeChronicles tells the fall of Judah under Zedekiah, then turns to the edict of Cyrus (Japhet, p. 8).
  2. 539 BCECyrus takes Babylon; the Cyrus Cylinder was written after this.
  3. c. 375–332 BCESilver “YHD” coins of the province of Yehud (dating from the Commons description).
  4. c. 460–320 BCEWindow for the last generation in Jehoiachin’s line (Japhet’s count).
  5. 2nd c. BCEHellenistic and Maccabean age; the latest date proposed for Chronicles.

7Part seven

Discussion

Ten questions with collapsible answers · about 25 minutes

Use these ten questions in a group of four to ten. Spend about two minutes on each before opening the answer. The answers give reasons and sources, not a single correct view.

Question 1. The Greek title Paraleipomena means “things left over.” What does the title assume about the book, and why does Japhet think it does not describe the book well?

It assumes that Chronicles is a supplement to Samuel and Kings. Japhet notes that the title names “what the translators regarded as its contents,” not its genre, and that it “may carry negative connotations” [Japhet 1993, p. 1]. The Hebrew title, “events of the days,” names a kind of writing (a chronicle) [Japhet 1993, p. 1]. Question for the group: does a supplement still tell a different story from the one it supplements? Table 1 suggests that it does.

Question 2. In 2 Sam 24:1 the anger of the LORD moves David to count the people; in 1 Chr 21:1 “Satan” does. What are two ways to read the change?

(a) The Chronicler removed God’s anger and gave the act to another agent, so that David “is presented as exclusively responsible” [Japhet 1993, p. 373]; Wellhausen listed it among many “improving touches” [Wellhausen 1885, p. 179]. (b) Japhet doubts that satan is a proper name, because it has no article; she reads “an adversary,” “the antithesis of Joab” [Japhet 1993, pp. 374–376]. The group may ask what each reading assumes about the Chronicler’s view of evil. disputed

Question 3. 1 Chr 20:1 keeps “But David tarried at Jerusalem,” though the story it introduces is gone. What does this show about the Chronicler’s method?

That he copies large pieces of text and cuts others, and that the join can fail. Wellhausen calls the result “meaningless” [Wellhausen 1885, p. 178]. Japhet: “A strict adherence to the original text and at the same time its adaptation according to various tendencies may result in internal incoherence” [Japhet 1993, p. 362]. Both agree the text is awkward; they differ on what the awkwardness proves.

Question 4. Did the author of Chronicles also write Ezra–Nehemiah? List two arguments for each side.

Yes: Zunz found it hard to give all of Ezra–Nehemiah to Ezra, and so gave both books to the Chronicler; later scholars restated the view in new forms, and Haran (1986) wrote on “the identical lines at the end of Chronicles and beginning of Ezra,” the plainest clue (Table 4) [Japhet 1993, pp. 3–4]. No: Japhet points to differences “in language, style, literary method,” and to “different and often opposite views about central issues of biblical history and theology” [Japhet 1993, p. 4]; Kalimi gives linguistic and other differences [ABR review of Kalimi]. Remember the second question, layers in the book itself, is separate (Figure 10). disputed

Question 5. Why is the date of Chronicles so hard to fix, and what does each proposed date change about how you read the book?

The book names no event of its own time, so every date is an inference from language, from the absence of Greek influence, and from the genealogy of Jehoiachin [Japhet 1993, pp. 24–26]. A date near 400 BCE makes it evidence for Persian-period Judah; a date near 250 BCE (Knoppers, as reported [ABR review of Knoppers]) makes it evidence for an early Hellenistic community. Figure 11 shows the spread. disputed

Question 6. Hezekiah’s tunnel, Manasseh in Esarhaddon’s list and Finkelstein’s estimate for Yehud: what can each test, and what can it not?

The tunnel can test whether 2 Chr 32:30 points to a real work and when it was built, but the studies disagree (Table 3; Case 1) [Frumkin et al. 2003] [Maeir and Chadwick 2013]. Esarhaddon’s list shows that Manasseh was an Assyrian vassal, but is silent about a captivity [Esarhaddon Prism B]. Finkelstein’s survey-based numbers limit the size of the province and so test the “great Israel” of the lists, but they depend on a density figure he chooses [Finkelstein 2010]. None of the three settles the book’s reliability as a whole. disputed

Question 7. Chronicles ends in mid-sentence with “let him go up.” What are two readings of that ending?

Kalimi reads it as a deliberate call for more exiles to return [ABR review of Kalimi]. A plainer reading is that the Chronicler quoted only as much of the edict as he needed to close the history on a note of new beginning, which fits Japhet’s description of the book as running “from beginning to ‘beginning’” [Japhet 1993, p. 8]. Table 4 puts the two texts side by side. disputed

Question 8. How should a historian use a book like Chronicles?

Two uses are possible: as evidence for the time it describes (the kings), and as evidence for the time it was written (the Persian or early Hellenistic community). Japhet insists that these be kept apart: sources, reliability and theology are “different considerations” [Japhet 1993, p. 18]. Wellhausen judged that in Chronicles “we find ourselves fully within the period of the scribes” [Wellhausen 1885, p. 227], which is to use the book mainly in the second way. A sound habit: for each claim, say which use it assumes, and what outside evidence, if any, can be set beside it.

Question 9. Why did a quarrel over a book of history become a quarrel over the age of the law of Moses? Use de Wette, p. 135, and Graf, p. 114.

The answer in the sources is a chain. Chronicles shows the Levitical worship as old, and old worship points to old law. De Wette says that without Chronicles “a host of troublesome proofs” for the early date of the Mosaic books “have disappeared” [de Wette 1806, p. 135]. Graf says that the traditional view rests “mainly” on Chronicles [Graf 1866, p. 114]. Wellhausen chose Chronicles as his starting point because the two histories can be compared and dated without first separating sources [Wellhausen 1883, p. 177]. Each step can be questioned: Japhet argues that sources, reliability and theology are separate questions [Japhet 1993, p. 18]. disputed

Question 10. Keil (1833) wrote that no deceiver’s book could belong to the canon; Wellhausen (1883) answered that a man like Keil “could even at the present day write a book of Chronicles.” What does the exchange show about how premises enter a historical argument?

Keil states his premise openly: his belief that the canon arose “under divine influence” and so cannot contain a deceiver’s book [Keil 1833, p. X]. Wellhausen does not argue with the belief. He argues that a writer who starts from a similar assumption about the past will tell the past as Chronicles does [Wellhausen 1885, p. 225]. The two disagree on what counts as evidence, and each names the other’s premise. A group can ask where de Wette, Zunz or Japhet state their premises, and whether any argument is free of one. The sources do not settle the answer. disputed

Glossary

Achaemenid empire
The Persian empire founded by Cyrus. It ruled Judah from 539 BCE until the Greek conquest (see the map in Part 6).
Apologetic
Writing that defends a belief or an authority against criticism. Keil called his 1833 book an “apologetic essay.”
Fraktur
The German Gothic (black-letter) type used in most German books of the nineteenth century. Machine reading of it is unreliable.
Imprimatur
The permit of a church authority to print a book, here a Catholic one (Movers, 1834).
Midrash
Interpretation and retelling of an older text. Zunz and Wellhausen both used the word of the Chronicler’s method.
Pentateuch
The first five books of the Bible, traditionally ascribed to Moses.
Priestly Code
The part of the Pentateuch with the laws on priests, sacrifice and ritual. Wellhausen held that it came after the exile and shaped Chronicles.
Privatdozent
In the German university, a lecturer licensed to teach but not yet a professor. De Wette was one at Jena in 1806.
Wissenschaft des Judentums
“The science of Judaism”: the study of Jewish history and literature by university methods, begun by Jewish scholars in nineteenth-century Germany. Zunz was one of its founders.
Canon
The list of books a community treats as authoritative.
Chronicler
The anonymous author of Chronicles, as scholars call him. Whether he was one person is part of the debate.
Deuteronomistic history
The books Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings, seen as one history shaped by the outlook of Deuteronomy.
Genealogy
A list of descent. 1 Chr 1–9 is almost all genealogy.
Hellenistic period
The age of Greek rule and influence after Alexander the Great (late fourth century BCE onward).
Iron Age II
The archaeological period roughly from 1000 to 586 BCE, the time of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah.
Late Biblical Hebrew
The form of biblical Hebrew used in the Persian period and after, with features that differ from earlier books.
Masoretic Text (MT)
The standard medieval Hebrew text of the Bible, edited by the Masoretes (scribes who fixed the vowels, accents and notes).
Paraleipomena
The Greek title of Chronicles, “things left over.”
Qumran, 4QSama
A scroll of Samuel from the caves at Qumran, near the Dead Sea. Its text sometimes agrees with Chronicles against the Masoretic Text.
Septuagint
The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.
Synoptic
“Seen together”: passages that run in parallel and can be set side by side, like Table 1.
Theodicy
An account of how a just God allows the evils of history.
Tradition history
A method that studies how texts grew by stages through repeated use and revision.
Vorlage
The exact text an author or translator worked from.
Writings (Ketuvim)
The third part of the Hebrew Bible, after the Torah and the Prophets. Chronicles is in it.
Yehud
The Aramaic name for Judah as a province of the Persian empire.
Yehud stamp impressions
Seal impressions on jar handles bearing the name “Yehud”; their spread is used to outline the province.

Corrections and points I could not confirm

These are the places where sources disagree or where I stopped short of a confirmation.

Corrected
  • Wellhausen’s book of 1878 is Geschichte Israels I; Prolegomena is the title from 1883, and the English translation of 1885 uses it [Encyclopedia.com].
  • The “one author” idea is not Noth’s: Zunz (1832) and Movers (1834) came first [Japhet 1993, p. 3].
  • Gramberg (1823) did not defend Chronicles against de Wette. A survey of 2021 lists his book among the attacks on de Wette [Ska 2021, p. 25, n. 33]; his own preface says he aims to justify the result of Gesenius and de Wette and to defend it against Dahler [Gramberg 1823, p. VII].
  • De Wette’s first volume is dated 1806 on its title page [de Wette 1806, title page]; a survey of 2021 gives 1807, the year of his second volume [Ska 2021, p. 20, n. 20].
  • Earlier in this page the timeline said that Movers reached the one-work view “independently” of Zunz. No source I opened says so (Ewald says it of himself), and the wording has been removed.
  • “Christian neglect” of Chronicles: not supported by anything I opened; the book was in every canon after the late Syriac doubts [Japhet 1993, p. 1].
Sources disagree
  • Japhet’s 1968 article: pp. 330–371 (JSTOR) or 332–72 (Japhet herself).
  • Ideology in Hebrew: 1977 (Hebrew University) or 1978 (Eisenbrauns); the English reprint: 2004 or 2009.
  • Her presidency of the World Union of Jewish Studies: 2006–2009 (Hebrew University) or 2005–2009 (IIAS).
  • Her commentary’s page count: 1,077 or 1,007, so none is given.
  • Knoppers’s date: “around the mid third century” in one review; I did not read the commentary.
  • De Wette’s death year: 1849 in the German National Library record and the NDB; the older ADB prints 1843 [NDB 1957] [GND].
  • De Wette’s essay in Japhet’s bibliography: listed as “Historisch-kritische Untersuchung über die Bücher der Chronik,” Halle 1823 [Japhet 1993, p. XXIV]. The title page I opened is Kritischer Versuch, Halle 1806. Whether hers is an error or another edition I could not tell.
  • Wellhausen’s ivy line: Ska cites “Prolegomena, 223,” and calls the 1878 book Prolegomena; in the 1883 German it is p. 237 and in the 1885 English p. 227. She may use a later edition.
  • Place of her birth: Tel Aviv in one record; no second source found.
Not confirmed
  • 558 parallel verses: from a 2025 paper citing a 1998 synopsis that I did not see [Endres et al., via arXiv].
  • Hebrew commentary on Chronicles, 2024: known from a publisher listing and from a notice that it was “in the press” [Am Oved listing].
  • The page range of Japhet’s 1985 article in JSOT 33.
  • Jerome’s prologue and the rabbinic references to the book’s names: through Japhet only.
  • Cross’s dates for his three stages: I have only Japhet’s summary, “sixth century” to the “fifth and fourth” [Japhet 1993, p. 6].
  • Whether Williamson, Willi, Noth and others held Ezra–Nehemiah to be by a different or the same author: Japhet’s survey does not say for each.
  • Yairah Amit’s position, and the arguments of Klein and Ben Zvi: no source opened.
  • Dahler, Gramberg’s chapters, Keil’s chapters and most of de Wette’s book: not read. Eichhorn’s review of 1807, Herz’s book of 1822 and Hengstenberg’s thesis of 1823: known only from Gramberg and Ska.
  • The nineteenth-century surveys Graham (1990), Mathias (1977) and Peltonen (1996): listed in Japhet’s bibliography (p. XIX) and in Ska’s notes, not opened.
  • Whether Wellhausen knew Zunz: a text search of the machine-read 1883 book finds no “Zunz”; I have not read every page.
  • Dillmann’s views: only as Wellhausen quotes them (p. 232).
  • The exact day of Japhet’s death in March 2024.
